request.system:
You are helping design a theme taxonomy for recorded calls at Aegis Cloud Security, a B2B SaaS company. The calls are customer support calls, calls between Aegis account managers and customers, and internal Aegis meetings. The taxonomy will be used by product and engineering leaders, support leaders and sales managers to see what the calls are about.

You will receive a batch of full call transcripts. Each starts with "=== call XXXXXX ===" where XXXXXX is the call id, followed by lines "Speaker (side): sentence". "side" is "customer" or "aegis_staff".

Task: read all the calls in the batch and propose CANDIDATE THEMES, plus a separate list of product areas.

A theme is what the call is about in terms of the issue or purpose (for example a kind of problem, a business event, or a kind of decision). A theme is NOT the product name and NOT the type of call.

Actionability test, which every theme must pass: you can name which one of these four stakeholders would act on a pattern of calls with this theme, and say in one sentence what they would do: "support lead", "sales / account manager", "product manager", "engineering lead". If you cannot, it is a topic label, not a theme; leave it out. Reject vague labels such as "discussion", "update" or "meeting".

For each theme return:
- name: short, plain, 2 to 5 words.
- definition: one sentence saying what makes a call belong to this theme.
- distinguishing: one sentence saying how it differs from the most similar theme in your list.
- owner: one of "support lead", "sales / account manager", "product manager", "engineering lead".
- actionable_because: one sentence on what the owner would do with a pattern of these calls.
- meeting_ids: the ids of EVERY call in this batch that substantially involve this theme, not only the best examples. A call may appear under more than one theme.
- evidence: up to 3 items, each {meeting_id, quote}. A quote must be copied EXACTLY, character for character, from a single line of that call. Do not paraphrase, shorten with "...", or join text from different lines. Use quotes from different calls where possible.

Rules:
1. Propose between 5 and 12 themes. Propose fewer if the calls support fewer. A theme needs at least 2 calls in this batch; a single call goes in other_note instead.
2. Base everything on the transcripts. Do not guess from names or invent details. Do not use any outside knowledge about Aegis.
3. product_areas: list the products, modules or product families that the speakers actually name in this batch, using the names as the speakers say them. For each give evidence (up to 2 items {meeting_id, quote}, same exact-copy rule) and meeting_ids of every call in the batch where that product is a main subject. Merge obvious spelling variants. Do not invent products that nobody names.
4. other_note: one or two sentences on calls that fit none of your themes and why. Write "none" if every call fits.
5. Every meeting_id you use must be an id that appears in this batch.

Return only JSON matching the schema.

Robert Langston (customer): Yeah, of course. We've got a lot to get through so let's, uh, let's just jump in.
Maria Santos (aegis_staff): Absolutely. And I'll just introduce Kevin — he's one of our Solutions Architects and I brought him on today because some of the questions Tanya sent over ahead of this call are a bit more technical and I wanted to make sure we had the right person in the room.
Kevin O'Brien (aegis_staff): Hey everyone, Kevin O'Brien. Happy to be here and, yeah, looking forward to the conversation.
Tanya Desai (customer): Hi Kevin. Tanya Desai, Security Engineering. I'll probably be the one throwing the hard questions at you.
Kevin O'Brien (aegis_staff): Ha, I'd expect nothing less. Bring it on.
Robert Langston (customer): So — look, Maria, I'm going to be straightforward with you. March has been... it's been a rough month for us in terms of our confidence in the platform. You know what I'm referring to.
Maria Santos (aegis_staff): The Detect outage. Yes, absolutely, and I want to address that head on. That's honestly one of the main reasons I pushed for this call rather than just sending an email.
Robert Langston (customer): Six hours, Maria. Six hours where we had zero visibility into threat monitoring. For a financial services firm, that's — I mean, do you understand what our risk exposure looks like in a window like that?
Maria Santos (aegis_staff): I do, and I'm not going to minimize that. It was a serious failure and I think you deserve a clear explanation of what happened and more importantly what's been done since. Kevin, do you want to walk through the technical side?
Kevin O'Brien (aegis_staff): Sure. So the root cause was a cascading failure in our event ingestion pipeline. Essentially there was a single point of failure in how events were being routed and processed — one node went down and it kind of pulled everything with it. It wasn't graceful at all.
Tanya Desai (customer): A single point of failure. In a production monitoring system. I have to be honest, that's a pretty basic architectural problem.
Kevin O'Brien (aegis_staff): You're right, and I'm not going to sit here and defend the original architecture. What I can tell you is that as of about a week and a half ago, we've implemented redundant processing nodes across the ingestion layer and we've added a circuit breaker pattern so that if one component degrades, it fails independently without taking down the whole pipeline.
Tanya Desai (customer): Can you send us documentation on those changes? Like, actual architecture diagrams, not just a summary email.
Kevin O'Brien (aegis_staff): Yes, absolutely. I can get you a technical brief with the updated architecture. I'd want to have our engineering team review it first just to make sure everything is accurate and nothing sensitive gets included, but yeah — that's a reasonable ask and we should be able to turn that around within the week.
Tanya Desai (customer): I'd also want to understand — what's the monitoring on the monitoring, so to speak? Like how do you detect that Detect itself is down?
Kevin O'Brien (aegis_staff): That's a really good question and it's something we've actually bolstered as part of the remediation. We have independent health checks running on the pipeline components now, separate from the pipeline itself, and those feed into our internal ops alerting. The goal is that we catch a degradation before it becomes a full outage.
Tanya Desai (customer): Okay. I mean, that sounds reasonable. Robert, I have more questions but I don't want to monopolize—
Robert Langston (customer): No, no, keep going. This is exactly what I need to hear.
Tanya Desai (customer): Alright. So the other thing I wanted to flag — and this is maybe a broader concern — is that during the outage we had no fallback. No secondary alerting, no cached state, nothing. Is there a recommended configuration we should have had in place that we didn't?
Kevin O'Brien (aegis_staff): Honestly, that's something we want to look at with you. There are configurations within Detect around alert persistence and, um, sort of offline buffering that can help, but those aren't always enabled by default and I think there may be a gap in how we onboarded your team to those features. I'd want to do a config review with you.
Robert Langston (customer): Let's put that on the action items list. I'll have Maria set that up separately.
Maria Santos (aegis_staff): Done. I'll reach out next week to schedule that with Tanya's team.
Robert Langston (customer): Okay. So let's talk about the renewal because that's technically why we're here. Our contract comes up end of Q2 and, uh, I'll be transparent — the board is asking questions. They want to know if we have alternatives.
Maria Santos (aegis_staff): I appreciate you being upfront about that. Can I ask — is the concern primarily around Detect, or is this a broader platform evaluation?
Robert Langston (customer): Mostly Detect, yeah. I mean — Protect has been solid, we've had no issues there. Identity is fine, works as expected. Comply is... we're still getting into it honestly, haven't fully utilized that module.
Maria Santos (aegis_staff): Actually, on that note — Comply v2 is launching April 7th and that's going to include on-demand reporting for SOC 2, PCI DSS, HIPAA, ISO 27001. Given you're in financial services that feels like it could be pretty relevant for your audit cycles.
Tanya Desai (customer): How on-demand are we talking? Like, can I run a PCI DSS report at 9pm on a Friday before an audit Monday morning?
Kevin O'Brien (aegis_staff): That's exactly the use case. Yes. You'd be able to generate the report, get a formatted output you can hand directly to auditors. We can demo that for you, probably sometime after the 7th once it's live.
Tanya Desai (customer): That would actually be useful. We have a PCI audit in June so the timing is... yeah, okay, that's worth a look.
Maria Santos (aegis_staff): Robert, I want to come back to the competitive piece you mentioned. I'm not going to pretend we don't know who you're talking to — SentinelShield's been pretty aggressive in financial services this year. I'd just ask that before any decision gets made, we get a chance to do a full side-by-side with you.
Robert Langston (customer): I think that's fair. Look, nobody wants to go through a platform migration — the integration effort alone is a headache. But I need to be able to justify the renewal to my leadership and right now the March outage is a pretty big thing sitting on the ledger.
Maria Santos (aegis_staff): Understood. What would make the renewal easier to justify? Is it the technical documentation Tanya mentioned, a formal incident post-mortem, SLA terms — what's most helpful?
Robert Langston (customer): Honestly? All of the above. But if I'm prioritizing — I want the post-mortem in writing, I want updated SLA language that actually has teeth around uptime for Detect specifically, and I want that config review done before we sign anything.
Maria Santos (aegis_staff): That's a clear list and I think those are all doable. I'll own getting the post-mortem document drafted — we have the internal one already, it's more about formatting it for external use. The SLA conversation I'll loop in our commercial team on, I want to make sure I'm not committing to terms I don't have authority on.
Robert Langston (customer): That's fine. Just don't let it sit for three weeks.
Maria Santos (aegis_staff): No, I hear you. I'll have a draft post-mortem to you by end of next week and I'll have an initial SLA proposal from our commercial team within two weeks. Does that work?
Robert Langston (customer): That works. Tanya, anything else from your side before we wrap?
Tanya Desai (customer): Just the architecture doc and scheduling the config review. Oh — and the Comply v2 demo. I actually do want to see that.
Maria Santos (aegis_staff): Great, I'll put all of that into a follow-up summary this afternoon. Robert, Tanya — thank you both for being candid today. I know this isn't the easiest conversation but I'd rather we're talking through it directly than not.
Robert Langston (customer): Yeah, same. Appreciate the transparency on your end too. Let's see where we land after the documentation comes through.
Maria Santos (aegis_staff): Sounds good. Talk soon.

evidence.quote: Our nightly backup jobs are taking, uh, somewhere between four and six hours to complete. They used to finish in under ninety minutes.

Granular file-level restore, like truly arbitrary path-based restore from within a snapshot, that's not currently a supported workflow in Protect.
